newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Murdoch's News surges in Australia on U.S. deals.
newsitem.headline: Murdoch's News surges in Australia on U.S. deals.

text.p: Shares in Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd roared back into favour on Thursday as investors re-rated the global media group after it announced two deals to buy and sell U.S. television assets worth US$3 billion.
News' shares surged as much as 38 cents or 6.5 percent to a new three month high of A$6.25 (US$4.69) in morning trade.
Analysts and brokers welcomed News' decision to sell its American Sky Broadcasting (ASkyB) satellite assets to the Primestar group of pay television operators for US$1.1 billion.
The analysts said the deal removed the risk of News having to plough more money into the new infrastructure.
"The Primestar deal comes as a relief given that News Corp has sunk considerable funds into ASkyB," said Bob Peters, media analyst at ANZ Investments.
"The Primestar deal takes out what essentially could have been a very big black hole for News Corp," added Vince Pepe, media analyst at ABN-Amro Hoare Govett.
The News and MCI Communications Corp ASkyB joint venture will receive US$1.1 billion or about 20 percent of Primestar non-voting stock and notes for the satellite assets.
News said the price was equal to its investment costs plus interest. News would not have any Primestar board seats and its role would be passive, Primestar said

The deal effectively ends Murdoch's hands-on involvement in U.S. satellite television, which had been seen as the crown jewel in News' global chain of satellite networks encompassing Asia's Star TV, Britain and Europe's BSkyB and Japan's JSkyB.
"As a result of the sale, News Corp will refocus its energies and resources in the U.S. on its core content and programming businesses," News said.

News' US$1.9 billion purchase of International Family Entertainment Inc, which runs family and children's cable television channels, was also welcomed because it was bought for cash rather than with News' non-voting preferred shares. The preferred stock rose up to 47 cents to A$5.28.
News' use of the preferred shares to buy marketing company Heritage Media Corp in March was savaged by investors worried about dilution and perceptions of an uncontrolled expansion.
"These deals will be a very big positive for News, firstly because they haven't used DPs (preferred shares) and they've conserved their cash," Pepe said.

News' March announcement of the Heritage deal triggered an 18-percent slide in News' preferred share price to a 15-month low. The slide hurt investors even more because it was set against a 10-percent rally in the Australian All Ordinaries index between March and mid-June.

Most analysts and brokers said they were unconcerned with the apparently high price paid by News' unit Fox Kids Worldwide for IFE, pointing to what appeared a strong fit between Fox Kids and IFE's children and family channels.

Standard and Poor's Corp put News' BBB credit rating on negative CreditWatch after the two deals, saying the price paid represented a very high multiple and that the venture would not be able to generate net cash flow given the expected debt financing involved.
But Murdoch said in a statement he was delighted with the acquisition.
"We expect the future combination of Fox Kids Network and The Family Channel will create a new force in world-wide family entertainment," he said.
